# Exodus 19 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1: Arrival at Sinai
Israel arrived at the Wilderness of Sinai in the third month (Sivan, roughly May–June), on the first day of that lunar month — about seven weeks after the Exodus. The timing coincides with what later became the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), which among other things celebrates the giving of the law. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-19-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

Ellicott notes this was about 45–47 days after leaving Egypt; the "same day" lit. means "on that day" — the first of the month. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

**Modern scholarship note:** Alan Cole (cited at Precept Austin) observes that "wilderness" here is not sandy desert but grazing country, not settled by man. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-19-commentary)

## v. 2: Camped before the mountain
Israel camped in front of Mount Sinai (identified by many with the plain Er-Rahah, facing Ras Sufsafeh). This fulfilled God's promise in Exodus 3:12 that they would worship God at this mountain. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-19-commentary)

Guzik notes that Israel remained here until Numbers 10 — over 57 chapters of Scripture cover what happened in the roughly one year they camped at Sinai. He also discusses the debated location, noting that Galatians 4:25 places Sinai in Arabia, and that some evidence points to Jebel al-Lawz in modern Saudi Arabia rather than the traditional Sinai Peninsula site. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

Precept Austin adds that "in front of" (Hebrew *neged*) means "prominently before" — Israel camped conspicuously before the mountain of God, the very place where Moses first met the LORD at the burning bush. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-19-commentary)

## v. 3: Moses went up to God; God calls with a message for "the house of Jacob…the sons of Israel"
Moses ascended the mountain and God called to him — perhaps meeting him partway, sparing him the full toil of the climb. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

The twofold title "house of Jacob" and "sons of Israel" is significant. Kaiser (cited at Precept Austin) says "house of Jacob" recalls their humble beginnings (cf. Gen 28:13), while "sons of Israel" reflects what they had become — a nation. Guzik adds that "house of Jacob" associates the nation with the weakest and least stable of the patriarchs; at this point they acted more like Jacob than Abraham or Isaac. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-19-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

## v. 4: "You have seen what I did to Egypt…I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself"
God prefaces the covenant offer by reminding Israel of His past mighty works — the plagues, the Red Sea deliverance. Ellicott says the reminder covers "the whole series of signs and wonders wrought in Egypt." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

**"Eagles' wings":** This metaphor conveys both strength and tender protective care. Ellicott explains that when young eagles are first fledged, the parent flies beneath them so the young can settle on its wings or back if needed. Guzik adds the traditional observation that an eagle carries its young on its back (not in its claws), so any arrow from a hunter must pass through the mother eagle first. Kaiser (quoted at Precept Austin) says the image speaks of "supernatural assistance given by God in a time of human incapability." Deuteronomy 32:11 develops the metaphor with "loving compassion, protection, strength, and watchfulness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-19-commentary; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

**"Brought you to Myself":** Ellicott says this means not simply "brought you to Sinai," but "brought you out of Egypt and its corrupting influences and led you back to My pure worship and true religion." Guzik stresses that the deliverance was for fellowship — God didn't deliver Israel so they could live apart from Him, but so they could be His people. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

## vv. 5–6: The Covenant Promise — "treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation"
These verses contain the heart of the Mosaic covenant proposal. Guzik notes that the covenant was greater than the law itself; it involved law, sacrifice, and the choice to obey and be blessed or to disobey and be cursed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

**"If you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant":** The condition. God offers blessing on the basis of obedience. John Piper (Desiring God) says God promises they will be His prized possession "if they keep his covenant," and these covenant blessings include intimate access to God and likeness to God. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-through-moses)

**"Treasured possession" (Hebrew *segullah*):** Ellicott explains the root means "to earn or acquire" — a valuable possession the owner has obtained by his own exertions. God views Israel as made His own by the mighty works of deliverance. The word is used here for the first time and later becomes a standard epithet for Israel (Deut 7:6; 14:2; 26:18; Ps 135:4; Mal 3:17). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

**"For all the earth is Mine":** Ellicott notes that while claiming a peculiar right in Israel, God does not mean to separate Himself from other nations. Israel is the "favoured son," but all nations are "children of the Most High." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

**"A kingdom of priests":** Ellicott explains this as all Israelites being both "kings and priests unto God" — kings as lords over themselves owing allegiance to God only; priests as entitled to draw near to God in prayer without an intermediary, to bring offerings and hold communion with Him. Pulpit Commentary renders it "a royalty of priests" — at once royal and priestly, all of them both. The LXX translates it *basileion hierateuma* ("a royal priesthood"), the phrase picked up in 1 Peter 2:9. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

Piper emphasizes that "the most striking privilege of the priests was intimate access to God" and that this privilege is heightened because it is a *royal* priesthood — priests in the service of the King. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-through-moses)

**"A holy nation":** Ellicott notes this refers primarily to official/consecrated holiness (being set apart for God), not merely personal holiness — though personal holiness is the natural outcome. Each Israelite was to be as near to God as the priests of other nations were or thought themselves. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

**New Testament application:** Multiple sources note that 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 1:6 apply this very language to the Church. Guzik says Peter reminds believers we are "a royal priesthood…a holy nation, His own special people." Piper makes the same connection. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-through-moses)

**Reformed perspective:** Ligonier notes that Exodus 19 records the enactment of the Mosaic covenant, one of several covenants through which the covenant of grace unfolds. The cleansing before God reveals His law "foreshadows the purification that Christ must give us before we will serve God with gladness." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-treasured-possession)

**Scholarly note:** Bible.org observes that Exodus 19:3-8 follows the pattern of ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaties: preamble (v.3), historical prologue (v.4), stipulations (v.5a), blessings for obedience (vv.5b-6), and acceptance in solemn assembly (vv.7-8). (https://bible.org/seriespage/15-god-s-purpose-his-people-exodus-191-25, from excerpt)

## vv. 7–8: The people's acceptance
Moses summoned the elders (the usual channel of communication) and laid before them "all these words." The people answered unanimously: "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

Ellicott observes there was "no hesitation, no diversity of opinion, no self-distrust" — in the glow of the great privileges offered, the difficulty of perfect obedience did not occur to them. Guzik (citing G. Campbell Morgan) says their answer "was sincere, but it was ignorant." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

Moses then "returned the words of the people unto the LORD" — acting as a true priestly intermediary. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

## v. 9: God will come in a thick cloud so the people will hear and trust Moses
God promises to appear in "the thickness of a cloud" — Ellicott says this was probably the pillar of cloud that had guided Israel. God must always veil Himself when speaking with man; even when He reveals Himself, He "dwells in the thick darkness" (2 Chron 6:1). The purpose was twofold: to impress the people with His awful presence, and to make them ready to submit to Moses and "believe him forever." Ellicott notes that this purpose was accomplished — the Law of Moses has remained the guide of Jewish life for over three millennia. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

The final clause "And Moses relayed to the LORD what the people had said" is a seeming repetition of v.8. Pulpit Commentary says such repetitions are "in the manner of archaic writers" and serve to emphasize the fact that the covenant acceptance was the necessary preliminary to all that follows. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

## vv. 10–11: Consecration and washing; ready for the third day
God required a two-day preparation before His descent on the third day. Ellicott notes that sanctification is twofold — outward and inward — but since no external command can secure inward sanctification, Moses was instructed to issue directions for outward purification (washing of clothes and persons), leaving it to the people's spiritual insight to recognize that external purity symbolised and required internal cleansing. The requirement of two full days taught that "man's defilement is, in the sight of God, very great." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

Pulpit Commentary adds: "Before man can be fit to approach God, he needs to be sanctified. The essential sanctification is internal; but, as internal purity and holiness cannot be produced at a given moment, Moses was ordered to require its outward symbol." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

On "the third day": Pulpit says there is no special significance to the number — the important point is the two days of purification. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

## vv. 12–13: Boundaries around the mountain; death penalty for trespassing
Moses was to erect a fence (artificial barrier) between the camp and the mountain. Anyone touching the mountain was to die. Ellicott notes that Ras Sufsafeh rises so abruptly from the plain that one can stand on the plain and yet touch the mountain — hence the need for a barrier. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

**"No hand shall touch him":** The meaning is that the transgressor must not be seized and arrested (which would require someone else to cross the boundary too). Instead, he must be killed by stoning or arrows from within the barrier. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

**"Whether man or beast":** Even an animal that strayed onto the mountain must die — though beasts are innocent of wrongdoing, the law required their slaughter when their owner's sin was appropriately punished through their loss, or when they had become polluted by contact with holy ground. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

Guzik observes that the death penalty taught Israel that "obedience is more important than their feelings" — even legitimate desires to draw near to God must be submitted to obedience. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

**"When the ram's horn sounds a long blast may they approach":** Ellicott and Pulpit both argue that the "they" is emphatic and does not refer to the people generally but to privileged persons (Moses, Aaron, and later the elders) — the people never do ascend. The trumpet signals the invitation for those authorized to come near. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

## vv. 14–15: Moses consecrates the people; "do not draw near to a woman"
Moses carried out the commands: the people washed their clothes. He added the instruction to abstain from marital relations. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

**"Do not draw near to a woman":** Ellicott explains this was the general sentiment of antiquity that ceremonial uncleanness attached even to chaste sexual connection — a view found in the Levitical law (Lev 15:18), among Egyptians, Greeks, Persians, and others. Guzik clarifies that the rest of Scripture does not teach any inherent uncleanness in marital relations; this command was peculiar to this event. God wanted the people to demonstrate their desire for purity by restraining even legitimate desires. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

## v. 16: Thunder, lightning, thick cloud, and the trumpet — the people trembled
On the third morning, the theophany began. Ellicott describes the phenomena: loud thunder (lit. "voices"), fierce lightning, fire streaming from the mountain to mid-heaven, dense smoke producing awful darkness, the mountain trembling as by continuous earthquake, and a trumpet blast — "so awful a manifestation has never been made at any other place or time." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

Pulpit Commentary forcefully argues that this was a "real theophany," not a mere storm or volcanic eruption which Moses exploited. "The only honest course is either to accept it as a plain record of plain (albeit miraculous) facts, or to reject it altogether as the fiction of a romancer." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

The trumpet (*shofar* / ram's horn) is the herald's signal calling attention to a proclamation. The sound came not from the camp but from heaven itself. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

## v. 17: Moses brought the people out to meet God at the foot of the mountain
An open space intervened between the camp and the fence. Moses led the people into this space, bringing them "as near as they might come to God." Ellicott says "the people" here means the chief of the people — the representatives. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

## v. 18: Mount Sinai enveloped in smoke; God descended in fire; the mountain quaked
The mountain "smoked, all of it" because the LORD descended in fire. Ellicott argues for real smoke (not just cloud appearing as smoke), because Deuteronomy 4:11 says "the mountain burned with fire." Pulpit likewise rejects the suggestion that thunder-clouds merely "had the appearance of smoke." The earthquake was a real earthquake, not mere thunder-vibration — compare Psalm 68:8, "Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

## v. 19: The trumpet grew louder; Moses spoke and God answered in thunder
The trumpet blast became longer and louder, more piercing and terrible. Pulpit Commentary suggests that at this point Moses could no longer endure to keep silence and "burst out in speech" — possibly the words recorded in Hebrews 12:21 ("I exceedingly fear and quake"), or words now lost to us. His speech had the effect of bringing the awful preparations to a close, and then "God answered him by a voice." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/19.htm)

Guzik notes that collectively, Israel heard the Lord God speak from Mount Sinai in an audible voice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

## v. 20: The LORD descended to the top; called Moses up
God came down in special presence to the summit (Ras Sufsafeh, not the higher Jebel Musa which is out of sight from the plain). Moses went up — requiring courage amid the thunder, lightning, fire, smoke, and earthquake. Yet, Guzik notes, Moses knew God not only in terms of awesome power but also in terms of gracious kindness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

## vv. 21–24: God warns again; priests must consecrate themselves; Moses protests
Despite the earlier warnings and the fence, God sent Moses back down with a fresh warning. Ellicott explains that an intention to "break through to gaze" must have been entertained by many. The priests in particular (the heads of families who exercised sacerdotal functions before the Levitical priesthood was instituted) seem to have been especially proud and rebellious — "accustomed to the exercise of sacred functions, they may have been inclined to regard their own purity as equal to that of Moses and Aaron" and may have resented their exclusion. They apparently neglected the purification rites, requiring a special command addressed to them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

Moses protested: "The people cannot come up Mount Sinai, for You solemnly warned us." Ellicott says Moses meant they cannot do so *unwittingly* — he did not contemplate intentional trespass, which is what God knew was contemplated. God overruled the objection and insisted: "Away! Get down and then come up, you and Aaron with you." Moses, "submissive as usual," obeyed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

## v. 25: Moses went down and spoke to them
Moses descended and delivered God's renewed warning. The result (implied) was that no attempt to break through the barrier was made. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/19.htm)

# Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

**Reformed / Covenant Theology (Ligonier):** The Mosaic covenant is understood within the broader covenant of grace. The law given at Sinai did not justify — only flawless obedience could do that. The cleansing rituals before the law's revelation "foreshadow the purification that Christ must give us before we will serve God with gladness." The Sinaitic covenant is seen as an administration of the covenant of grace, not a republication of a covenant of works for Israel. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-treasured-possession)

**Baptist (John Piper / Desiring God):** Piper emphasizes that God's promises in vv.5-6 are conditional: "if you keep my covenant." He highlights the privilege of intimate access to God ("the most striking privilege of the priests") and that the blessings of being God's "prized possession" apply to New Covenant believers through 1 Peter 2:9. The emphasis is on God's sovereign grace in making Israel His own, and on the joyful duty of obedience in response. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-through-moses)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik draws a strong contrast between Mount Sinai (fear, terror, barriers, law, exclusion) and Mount Zion under the New Covenant (love, forgiveness, invitation, grace). He stresses that believers now "don't approach God as trembling people kept at a distance, but as those made welcome through Christ." At the same time, the practical lessons from Sinai remain: we must receive God's word, be set apart, be cleansed, respect boundaries, and restrain the flesh — but through Christ's blood, not from behind barriers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-19/)

# What Could Not Be Found

- **Methodist/Wesleyan** and **Lutheran** tradition-specific commentaries on this chapter were not accessible in the searches and fetches completed.
- **Catholic and Orthodox** readings (e.g., from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) were not retrieved.
- **Modern scholarly / critical views** (e.g., bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes) were not accessed.
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** (StudyLight.org) was seen only in search excerpt, confirming the standard Baptist reading that the principles "apply likewise to God's people today" and that "a kingdom of priests" means Israel would be "both kings and priests," cross-referencing 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 1:6. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-19.html)
